title: Latency vs Throughput
summary: Precise vocabulary for speed and capacity — percentiles, tail latency amplification, and Little's Law — used to reason about every design decision.

slides.markdown:
**Latency** is how long one request takes; **throughput** is how many requests the system handles per second. They sound related but you can optimize one while hurting the other.

Think of a highway: latency is how long one car takes to cross it; throughput is how many cars cross per minute. Adding lanes raises throughput without changing any single car's trip time. This topic gives you the precise vocabulary — percentiles, tail latency, Little's Law — for reasoning about "fast" in an interview.

slides.sectionTitle: Latency vs throughput: two different axes of "fast"
slides.markdown:
**Latency** is the time from request to response for a single unit of work, usually measured in milliseconds. **Throughput** is the rate of work completed, usually measured in requests-per-second (or QPS).

A batch job can have terrible latency (each job takes 10 minutes) but excellent throughput (thousands run in parallel). A real-time trading system needs the opposite: low latency per request matters more than how many run concurrently.

Before optimizing, name which one the product actually needs — the fixes for each are often different, sometimes opposed.

slides.sectionTitle: Percentiles: why averages lie (p50 vs p99 vs p999)
slides.markdown:
**Average latency** hides the worst experiences. If 99 requests take 10ms and one takes 5,000ms, the average is about 60ms — looks fine, but one in a hundred users waited five full seconds.

**Percentiles** fix this: **p50** (median) is the typical request, **p99** is the request slower than 99% of others, **p999** captures the rarest, worst outliers. Interviewers care about p99/p999 because at scale — a million requests a day — the "rare" 1% is 10,000 real users having a bad time every single day.

Always ask "which percentile?" before agreeing to a latency target.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: latency distribution and the long tail
slides.markdown:
![Latency distribution showing the long tail](assets/latency-long-tail.svg)

Most requests cluster near the median, but the distribution has a **long tail** — a small fraction of requests take dramatically longer, often due to garbage collection pauses, cache misses, lock contention, or a slow downstream dependency.

The tail is where SLA violations live: a system can have a great median and still miss its p99 target if the tail is fat.

slides.sectionTitle: Tail latency amplification: why one slow dependency ruins the whole request
slides.markdown:
If a single request fans out to call 10 downstream services, and each has a 1% chance of hitting its own slow p99, the *combined* chance that at least one of the 10 is slow is roughly 1 - 0.99^10 ≈ 10% — ten times worse than any individual service's tail.

This is **tail latency amplification**: the more services a request touches, the more likely it hits somebody's bad day. It's why fan-out architectures (search, feeds, dashboards) fight tail latency harder than simple CRUD services, and why techniques like hedged requests and timeouts-with-fallback exist.

slides.sectionTitle: Little's Law: relating concurrency, latency, and throughput
slides.markdown:
**Little's Law** states: `L = λ × W` — the average number of requests in the system (L) equals the arrival rate (λ, throughput) times the average time each spends in the system (W, latency).

Rearranged, it tells you something concrete: if your server can hold 100 requests in flight at once (concurrency limit) and average latency is 50ms, max sustainable throughput is `100 / 0.05s = 2,000 requests/sec`. Push more traffic than that and requests start queueing, which *increases* latency, which lowers your effective throughput further — a feedback loop worth naming in an interview.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: optimizing for latency vs optimizing for throughput
slides.markdown:
The techniques that help one can actively hurt the other.

| | Optimize for latency | Optimize for throughput |
|---|---|---|
| Batching | Avoid — batching adds wait time | Embrace — amortizes per-request overhead |
| Concurrency | Keep request paths short and direct | Maximize parallel work in flight |
| Caching | Cache aggressively per-request | Cache to reduce backend load overall |
| Example system | Trading engine, autocomplete | Log ingestion, batch ETL |

**How to decide:** ask what the user actually feels — a human waiting on a click needs latency; a pipeline processing a queue needs throughput. Some systems (checkout) need both, which usually means paying for more capacity rather than picking one.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: quoting average latency as your SLA
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our average latency is 80ms, so we're meeting our 100ms SLA."

**Why it's wrong:** an average can look great while a meaningful slice of users have a terrible experience — 80ms average is consistent with 95% of requests at 50ms and 5% at 700ms, which is a real, complaint-generating problem an average completely hides.

**Correct model:** SLAs should be defined and measured on a **percentile** (commonly p99 or p95), not the average. "p99 under 200ms" tells you the worst-case experience almost every user will actually see.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-level nuance: coordinated omission silently hides your worst latency
slides.markdown:
A subtle measurement bug produces percentiles that look better than reality: **coordinated omission**. If a load-testing tool sends the next request only *after* the previous one finishes, then during a slow patch — say the server stalls for 2 seconds — the tool simply sends fewer requests during that stall, instead of recording that every request which *should* have been sent during those 2 seconds was effectively waiting the whole time. The stall's damage disappears from the measurement because the requests that would have captured it were never sent.

The fix is measuring against a fixed, independent schedule — send requests at a constant target rate regardless of how the previous one is doing, and record how late each one actually starts, not just how long it takes once it starts. Tools built for this (`wrk2`, HdrHistogram-based benchmarks) exist specifically because naive load-testing tools (early JMeter and ab usage patterns) get this wrong by default.

The senior-level tell: an engineer who reports "our load test shows p99 of 40ms" without being able to say whether the test coordinated on omission is reporting a number that might be meaningfully optimistic — the gap between measured and real p99 during a real stall can be an order of magnitude.
